sentences.text: Pachycephalosaurus was among the last non-avian dinosaurs to exist before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
This animal reached 4.5 meters in length and weighed between 370 and 450 kilograms, featuring a large bony dome on its skull up to 25 cm thick.
It was a bipedal herbivore with long strong legs, small arms that had five fingers, and a short skull with large, forward-facing eye sockets suggesting binocular vision.
Fossils of Pachycephalosaurus have been found in Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Alberta, mostly within the Lance and Hell Creek Formations of the northwestern United States.
The bone fragment for Tylosteus ornatus was collected by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden from the head of the Missouri River, with its Cretaceous age indicated the following year.
The bone fragment was doubtfully identified as a dinosaur by Oliver Perry Hay in 1902 and definitively identified as a dinosaur by Charles Whitney Gilmore in 1928.

Donald Baird and John R. Horner independently identified the Tylosteus holotype ANSP 8568 as a squamosal from a Pachycephalosaurus skull, while Baird suggested that Joseph Leidy's identification of the discovery location as the head of the Missouri River was a misunderstanding of the confluence of the Jefferson and Madison Rivers.
Pachycephalosaurus is the largest known pachycephalosaur, characterized by an extremely thick, slightly domed skull roof.

The skull structure suggests Pachycephalosaurus used its head as a battering ram for defense or combat with other members of its species, and a 2012 study indicated that cranial pathologies in a Pachycephalosaurus specimen were likely caused by agonistic behavior.
Pachycephalosaurus coexisted with diverse dinosaurs including ceratopsians, hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs, and theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
Pachycephalosaurus is the most famous member of the clade Pachycephalosauria, and the genus Pachycephalosaurus was established by Brown and Schlaikjer in 1943.

The genus Tylosteus is considered synonymous with Pachycephalosaurus, and in 1986, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature affirmed Pachycephalosaurus as the conserved name and rejected Tylosteus.
Pachycephalosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period.

The hypothesis that Pachycephalosaurus used its skull for head-butting has been disputed in recent years. The synonymy of Stygimoloch with Pachycephalosaurus is disputed because specimens from each genus come from different time periods in rock layers. Researchers have debated whether Stygimoloch and Dracorex are distinct species or growth stages of Pachycephalosaurus. Some researchers suggest Stygimoloch might represent a different species, Pachycephalosaurus spinifer, rather than a growth stage.
